series.title: Path of Knowledge
series.premise: One idea per episode, taken from a question to a visual argument, in about two minutes.
series.audience: Curious adults who like mathematics explained honestly.
series.visual_motif: One thin accent line carries the argument: it becomes the curve, the pair, or the count.

episode.title: Why 23 people are enough for a shared birthday
episode.thesis: The birthday problem is about pairs, not people: 23 people create 253 pairs, so a 50% coincidence is unremarkable.
episode.question: Why does a 50% chance of a shared birthday arrive at only 23 people, when there are 365 days to choose from?
episode.audience: Adults comfortable with basic probability who have never worked through the birthday problem.
goals: Replace the one-person-against-everyone framing with pairwise counting.
Derive the exact probability from the complement.
Read the curve: 50.7% at 23 people, 99% at 57.
key_points: Counting the complement is easier than counting matches.
Pairs grow quadratically, which is why intuition fails early.
misconceptions: The calculation compares one person with the other 22.
A 50% result implies birthdays are not uniformly distributed.
visuals: Exact probability curve against group size, crossing one half at 23.
The complement product subtracted from one.
episode.next_teaser: Where else does counting pairs beat counting people?

notation: Write n for the number of people and D = 365 for the number of days.
Use P for probability; do not mix percentages and fractions inside one formula.
accuracy.conventions: Percentages to one decimal place. Decimal point, not comma.
sources: Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1 (birthday problem)
Exact values recomputed in the episode: P(23) = 0.507297, P(57) = 0.990122
